To argue means one of two things, and understanding both is the key to truly knowing this word.

First meaning: To disagree with someone by expressing your different opinion out loud, using words.

Second meaning: To give reasons to support or oppose a position — calmly, logically, and on purpose.

These two meanings feel quite different in tone, but they share a common core: you are actively putting your view forward, not just sitting quietly with it. Arguing is always active. You are saying something. You are pushing a point.

This is the meaning most people reach for first. When two people argue, they disagree about something and they express that disagreement to each other — often with frustration, raised voices, or strong emotion.

For example:

  • "The couple argued about money."
  • "My brother and I always argue over what to watch on TV."
  • "Stop arguing and just listen to me!"

Notice a few things here. Arguing in this sense involves at least two people. It is not a one-sided speech. Each person is pushing back against the other. There is tension. There is conflict.

Importantly, arguing in this sense is done with words, not fists. This is a crucial distinction. When people argue, they are using language — even if that language is loud, unkind, or emotional. The moment it becomes physical, we stop calling it arguing.

Also notice that arguing does not require anyone to be right. Two people can argue all afternoon and both be partly right, or both be wrong. Arguing is about the disagreement itself, not about who wins.

What are they disagreeing about? In everyday life, people argue about almost anything — money, relationships, politics, whose turn it is to do the dishes, what really happened in the past. The subject of an argument is limitless.

This is where the word becomes more sophisticated, and it is just as important as the first meaning.

In this sense, to argue means to make a case for something using reasons and evidence. There is no fighting here. No raised voices. You are simply building a logical case to show why something is true, correct, or worth believing.

A lawyer argues in court — presenting evidence and reasoning to convince the judge or jury. A scientist argues in a paper — using data to support a conclusion. A student argues in an essay — using facts and logic to defend a position.

For example:

  • "She argued that the new policy would reduce crime."
  • "He argued for stricter environmental laws."
  • "The report argues against expanding the highway."

In this sense, you can argue for something (you support it with reasons), or argue against something (you present reasons why it is wrong or harmful). You can also argue that something is the case — meaning you claim it is true and give your reasons.

Notice that this meaning does not require another person to disagree with you in real time. A book, an essay, or a speech can "argue" something. The argument is in the reasoning itself.

The same word — argue — can therefore feel completely different depending on context.

"They argued for three hours" might mean they were in a heated, emotional conflict. Or it might mean two scholars were having a deep, structured intellectual debate. The word itself does not always tell you which tone is meant. Context — the situation, the relationship between people, the surrounding words — fills that in for you.

Often, though, real-life arguments are somewhere in the middle: people genuinely care about what they believe, and that emotion mixes with reasoning. A parent arguing with a teenager about curfew is both emotional and presenting reasons. The two meanings blend constantly in real life.

To use this word correctly, you need to know what naturally follows it.

Argue with someone — this signals conflict or disagreement between people.
"Don't argue with me."
"She argued with her boss."

Argue about / over something — this tells you what the disagreement is about.
"They argued about politics."
"We argued over who was responsible."

Argue for something — you support it; you present reasons in its favour.
"He argued for a shorter working week."

Argue against something — you oppose it; you present reasons why it should not happen.
"She argued against the proposal."

Argue that... — you state a position and imply that you have reasons for it.
"The professor argued that the experiment was flawed."
"I would argue that this decision is a mistake."

Knowing what a word is not is just as valuable as knowing what it is.

Argue vs. Disagree: To disagree simply means to hold a different opinion. You can disagree in silence — entirely in your own head. But to argue, you must express that disagreement out loud or in writing. Arguing is active. Disagreeing is not.

Argue vs. Fight: In everyday English, people sometimes use "argue" and "fight" interchangeably for verbal conflicts. But strictly speaking, a fight can be physical, while an argument is always verbal. Also, a fight tends to imply more raw aggression. An argument, even an emotional one, still involves words and (usually) attempts to make a point.

Argue vs. Discuss: A discussion is open and exploratory. People share views without necessarily trying to defeat each other. An argument, even in its intellectual sense, involves taking a position and defending it. There is more pushback, more opposition, more of a sense that someone is trying to win or prove something.

Argue vs. Debate: A debate is a formal, structured version of arguing. You can argue casually and spontaneously. Debates have rules, turns, and structure. All debating involves arguing, but not all arguing is a formal debate.

Argue vs. Quarrel: A quarrel is almost entirely emotional — often petty, personal, and driven more by feeling than by reason. An argument, even in its most heated form, tends to involve at least some attempt to make a point. Quarrelling is the messier, more irrational cousin.

When you argue — in either sense — you are not simply stating something. You are defending it. There is resistance involved, either from another person or from the difficulty of the subject itself. This is what gives the word its energy. To argue is to push — with your voice, your words, your reasoning — because you believe something and you want others to see it too.

This is why "I argue that kindness matters" feels stronger than "I think kindness matters." The word "argue" signals that you have thought about it, that you are prepared to back it up, and that you are ready for pushback.

The verb argue captures a uniquely human act: the act of using words to push a point. Whether that looks like two friends raising their voices over a misunderstanding, or a scholar carefully dismantling a theory with evidence, the same word covers it all — because both share a common soul. In both cases, someone cares about what they believe, and they are not staying quiet about it.
